title: Governor of Oklahoma

context.text: Open seat: Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt is term-limited. Oklahoma governors serve four-year terms and may serve eight years in total.

Republican primary (June 16, 2026): Attorney General Gentner Drummond led the first round with 26.3%, ahead of former state Sen. Mike Mazzei (26.0%), Chip Keating (18.5%), Jake Merrick (14.5%) and Charles McCall (11.8%). Mazzei won the August runoff, 50.3% to 49.7%.
Democratic primary: House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson won with 74.9%, ahead of former state Sen. Connie Johnson (22.3%) and Arya Azma (2.8%).
Oklahoma's lieutenant governor is elected separately, not as a running mate: T.W. Shannon (R) and Kelly Forbes (D) are on the ballot for that office.
Three independents also appear on the ballot for governor: Robert E. Brooks Sr., Orlando Lynn Bush and Jerry Griffin, as listed by the State Election Board.

candidates.name: Mike Mazzei
candidates.ballotNote: Won the Republican nomination in the August runoff. Oklahoma's lieutenant governor is elected separately.
candidates.currentRole: Chairman and CEO, Trinity Strategic Wealth; former state senator and Secretary of Budget

priorities.text: A three-phase plan to make Oklahoma a no-income-tax state within six years and to eliminate property taxes for seniors 65 and older and veterans.
Offsetting tax cuts with a Department of Government Efficiency and an Office of State Finance and Fiscal Responsibility to audit agency spending.
Education: hiring a statewide literacy director, a more transparent education process for parents, higher teacher pay and expanded pathways into teaching.

positions.summary: Says life begins at conception and that he opposes abortion in all circumstances, according to News 9's candidate guide.

record.text: Authored S.B. 1894 (2006), the Oklahoma Pension Legislation Actuarial Analysis Act; the conference report was adopted 45–0 in the Senate and 97–0 in the House, and the governor approved it on June 7, 2006.
Authored S.B. 334 (2006), which would have repealed Oklahoma's estate tax; it passed the Senate 46–0 and the House 79–17 but died in a conference committee on May 26, 2006.

candidates.name: Cyndi Munson
candidates.ballotNote: Oklahoma's lieutenant governor is elected separately.
candidates.currentRole: Oklahoma State Representative, District 85 (since 2015); House Minority Leader (2022–2026)

priorities.text: Raising the minimum wage for all Oklahomans and pay raises for state employees.
priorities.quote: She will make it a top priority as Governor to raise the minimum wage for all Oklahomans and provide pay raises for state employees.

priorities.text: Fully funding public schools, teacher pay raises, expanding Oklahoma's Promise and free school meals, and repealing the state's Parental Choice Tax program.
Targeted tax relief for lower- and middle-income families rather than further income tax cuts, and a first-day moratorium on new data center construction.

positions.summary: Supports a state question to overturn Oklahoma's abortion ban and write abortion access into the state constitution.
Says she has authored legislation to raise the minimum wage and would make raising it a top priority as governor.
Would repeal the state's Parental Choice Tax program, which she says diverts nearly $300 million of public money to private schools.
Opposes further across-the-board income tax cuts that she says benefit high earners, but proposes expanding existing tax credits for lower- and middle-income earners rather than raising taxes.

record.text: Voted no on SJR 50, a proposed constitutional amendment on Medicaid funding; it passed the House 69–18.
Voted no on SB 1546, an Equal Opportunity Education Scholarship Act bill; it passed the House 55–27.
Voted no on SB 237, which created an ad valorem tax exemption for manufacturing facilities including battery energy storage systems; it passed the House 74–16.
Voted no on SB 1618, a pretrial-release bill requiring courts to conduct certain risk assessments; it passed the House 62–23.
Voted yes on HB 4408, which required data on savings and averted costs from the Oklahoma Smart Justice Reform Act (State Question 780); it passed the House 67–30.

candidates.name: Robert E. Brooks Sr.

priorities.text: Let the People Decide; Let the People See; Ask the People Before Major Decisions; Protect the Constitutional Rights of Every Oklahoman (his four campaign promises).
Affordable healthcare options, including a public option open to every Oklahoman.
A tax reform plan with a goal of eliminating personal income tax on household income up to three times the state median.

positions.summary: Proposes letting every Oklahoma resident buy into a SoonerCare-style public plan, with income-based premiums.
positions.quote: every Oklahoma resident would have the opportunity to purchase a SoonerCare-style health plan.

positions.summary: Says education funding should follow the student, with accountability for public funds.
positions.quote: Education funding should follow the student while maintaining transparency and accountability for taxpayer dollars.

positions.summary: Supports border security and consistent enforcement, with a voluntary registration process and enforcement focused first on public-safety risks.
positions.quote: A nation has both the right and the responsibility to secure its borders, enforce its laws fairly, and treat every person with dignity.

statements.quote: Higher-income taxpayers would have opportunities to reduce remaining Oklahoma income-tax liability through qualifying Oklahoma spending and investment.
Our answer is an Oklahoma all-of-the-above energy strategy.
statements.context: In his 'People's Oklahoma Energy Partnership' plan

statements.quote: families could qualify for performance-based childcare assistance or educational stipends.

candidates.researchNotes: Positions and statements come from the plan pages of his campaign site (votewethepeople.com), which has plans on healthcare, immigration, education, taxes and energy. No abortion, gun-law or minimum-wage position found.

candidates.name: Orlando Lynn Bush
candidates.researchNotes: No campaign website, questionnaire answers or public statements on issues were found for Bush; he remains a minimal entry.

researchNotes: The slate was checked against the Oklahoma State Election Board's 2026 Candidate List Book (candidate filing, official): governor filers were nine Republicans, three Democrats (Munson, Arya, Connie Johnson) and three independents (Griffin, Brooks, Bush). Primary and runoff results come from Wikipedia's tabulation of the Election Board's results; News 9 (October 6) lists the general-election field as Mazzei (R), Munson (D) and the three independents. Oklahoma elects the lieutenant governor separately, so there are no running mates. Ballotpedia blocked automated access. Mazzei's campaign website could not be loaded; his priorities and abortion position come from News 9's candidate guide, and the bill records from the Oklahoma Legislature's bill pages (2006 session). Munson's record is House third-reading roll calls checked against the official oklegislature.gov vote pages; her 2025 votes are not in the snapshot. The three independents have minimal public footprint; their occupations (farmer, former Tulsa school board member) come from Wikipedia. Munson's tax position is marked mixed because she opposes broad income tax cuts but proposes no tax increases. Update: Brooks's positions come from the plan pages of his campaign site (votewethepeople.com); his entry is now 'basic'. Bush and Griffin have no public issue statements found.
